summary: This memo describes a gateway that translates interactively between the Internet file transfer protocol FTP and the OSI file transfer protocol FTAM, so users of one can reach files on the other. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Two computer worlds moved files using different rules. This paper describes a translator that stands between them so each side can get files from the other. It is historic.

questions: how to translate between ftp and ftam
what is the ftp ftam gateway
how does the gateway translate between ftp and ftam
why is the ftp ftam gateway historic
subtitle: A gateway that translates file transfer requests between FTP and the OSI standard FTAM protocol.

tldr.problem: During the 1990s transition from TCP/IP to OSI, two incompatible file transfer protocols existed: FTP (for TCP/IP) and FTAM (for OSI). Users of one could not easily access files on systems using the other.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies an application-layer gateway that runs both FTP and FTAM protocol stacks and translates protocol commands in both directions, letting FTP clients access FTAM servers and vice versa without either side needing modification.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is historic. The approach was never widely deployed because the TCP/IP suite achieved dominance before OSI became established, and FTAM remained an academic exercise rather than a practical protocol.

today: RFC 1415 is Historic and was never widely deployed. The gateway was fielded on MILNET in the late 1980s and included in the ISO Development Environment, but the dominance of TCP/IP over OSI meant FTAM never became a practical protocol outside specialized government and research networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The FTP-FTAM Gateway Specification describes a protocol translator that bridges the File Transfer Protocol (FTP, used on TCP/IP networks) and the File Transfer, Access and Management (FTAM) protocol (the OSI standard for file transfer).

The gateway is an application-layer translator that runs both FTP and FTAM protocol stacks simultaneously. It accepts connections from either FTP clients or FTAM initiators, translates their requests into the opposite protocol, and handles the responses. The goal is to let users of one world access file services in the other, with minimal changes to either side.

The RFC specifies how the gateway resolves names (FTP uses domain names, FTAM uses X.500 distinguished names), how it maps protocol commands, and how it handles error conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different networks—one using FTP, one using FTAM—could not talk to each other. This gateway sits in the middle and speaks both languages, translating requests back and forth so either side can get files from the other.

sections.title: Gateway Architecture and Operation
sections.content:
The gateway implements a protocol translator architecture with three main components:

  • FTP server side: accepts connections from FTP clients
  • FTAM initiator side: sends requests to remote FTAM responders
  • Application logic: translates between the two protocols

The gateway provides two modes of operation. In FTP-initiated mode, an FTP client connects to the gateway, identifies a remote FTAM server (by its distinguished name), and the gateway bridges the connection. In FTAM-initiated mode, an FTAM initiator connects to the gateway to access a remote FTP server.

A key design principle is that files are streamed through the gateway rather than stored on it, which reduces storage requirements and latency.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway has two doors—one for FTP clients, one for FTAM clients. When someone walks in one door with a request, the gateway translates it and sends it out the other door to the destination. The file data flows straight through without staying on the gateway.

sections.title: Name Resolution and Addressing
sections.content:
FTP and FTAM use completely different naming schemes, making this a central problem for the gateway.

FTP addressing: FTP clients identify a server by its domain name and IP address. The gateway uses the Domain Name System to resolve these.

FTAM addressing: FTAM clients use X.500 Directory Services and distinguish names (like c=US@o=Company@ou=Services@cn=ftam-server). The gateway must query the X.500 directory to obtain the presentation address.

More transparent mode: To reduce user friction, FTP hosts providing FTAM services can be registered in DNS pointing to the gateway, or FTAM hosts can be registered in X.500 with the gateway's address, hiding the gateway from the user.

The specification assumes X.500 Directory Services are available. It also supports User Friendly Names (informal names like server, company, us) as an alternative to formal distinguished names.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP says "go to example.com on IP 1.2.3.4". FTAM says "find the file service for our company in the directory". The gateway has to learn both naming systems and translate between them.

sections.title: Protocol Mapping and State Machines
sections.content:
The gateway maintains separate state machines for FTP-initiated and FTAM-initiated services. Each defines the legal states and transitions the gateway can make.

For FTP-initiated service, states include: Initial (waiting for USER command), Wait-for-PASS, Wait-for-PAddress (resolving the destination), Wait-for-Connection, and Wait-for-ClientCmd/Wait-for-ResponderCmd (passing commands between sides).

For FTAM-initiated service, similar states exist, starting from receiving F-INITIALIZE and resolving the FTP server address.

The mapping between protocols is complex and not always one-to-one. Some FTP commands map to multiple FTAM functions, some map to none. For example, FTP's QUIT command maps to FTAM's F-P-ABORT or F-U-ABORT plus F-TERMINATE. This asymmetry means some functionality is unavoidably lost.

The gateway must also map diagnostic messages and error codes between the two protocols, which is inherently lossy.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway follows a recipe for each command it receives: if it is FTP's LIST command, it does these five FTAM steps. If it is FTAM's F-OPEN, it does these FTP steps. Some recipes are complex because the protocols do not match up perfectly.

sections.title: Supported Document Types and Lost Functionality
sections.content:
The gateway supports three document types:

  • FTAM-1 (unstructured text) maps to FTP ASCII
  • FTAM-3 (unstructured binary) maps to FTP 8-bit binary
  • NBS-9 (directory listing) maps to FTP directory listing

As is inevitable when translating between two protocols, some functionality is lost:

  • Diagnostics may not translate precisely from one protocol to another
  • FTAM's record-level access (reading part of a file) may not be fully emulated
  • FTAM attributes not supported by FTP cannot be transferred
  • The gateway does not support the FTP three-node model or stateless FTAM features

The specification was based on the NIST Stable Implementation Agreements for FTAM Phase 2 (March 1992) and assumes POSIX file naming conventions on both sides.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every trick that FTAM can do works on FTP and vice versa. If you ask the gateway for something only FTAM supports, it has to say "sorry, I cannot do that." The gateway picks the most common operations and makes those work.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC provides several implementation guidelines.

Robustness: If one side drops a connection, the gateway must promptly notify the other side with an appropriate error (a 426 reply for FTP, an F-P-ABORT with diagnostic 1011 for FTAM).

Well-known port: The gateway should listen on a standard TCP port for FTP connections and be registered in OSI directories for FTAM connections.

Gateway processes: A single gateway machine can run multiple listener processes to handle concurrent connections.

POSIX file naming: The gateway assumes hierarchical directory structures with POSIX naming conventions, which limits support for systems using different file organization.

The RFC also notes that the gateway has higher implementation and maintenance burden than a single-protocol system, as it must keep both protocol implementations current.
sections.plainLanguage: To run a gateway, you need good error handling (if one side breaks, tell the other), a stable network service, and the willingness to maintain two protocol implementations instead of one.

viz.caption: Two ways to use the gateway

left.title: FTP-initiated
left.desc: FTP client initiates, gateway acts as FTAM initiator to reach FTAM server.

right.title: FTAM-initiated
right.desc: FTAM initiator initiates, gateway acts as FTP client to reach FTP server.
